001 - Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book a: Seinfeld was the massively popular 1990s NBC sitcom about four self-absorbed friends in New York, famously self-described as 'a show about nothing.' Its characters, who fuss obsessively over trivia while shrugging off morality, turn out to be ideal test cases for serious questions: Can George ever become virtuous, or is he doomed by habit? Is Elaine a feminist icon? Is Kramer Kierkegaard's aesthete, fleeing commitment in an endless rotation of schemes? Even the show's 'nothing' becomes a question about whether nothingness can be something.
003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcom: The Matrix (1999) is the landmark science-fiction film in which hacker Neo discovers that ordinary life is a computer simulation fed to humans whose bodies power the machines. The red pill/blue pill choice made it the perfect hook for philosophy: How do you know you are not deceived, right now? The essays here read Neo as Socrates waking up Athens, his unplugging as Plato's cave allegory, and the film as a Rorschach blot in which skeptics, Christians, and Buddhists alike can find their questions.
004 - Buffy the Vampire Slayer - Fear an: Buffy the Vampire Slayer (1997-2003) is the cult-favorite TV series about a teenage girl fated to hunt vampires while navigating school, friendship, and love in the demon-plagued town of Sunnydale. Beneath the monsters it took morality seriously: does the just person really live better than the unjust, as Faith's collapse into evil suggests? Is Buffy's identity relational rather than solitary? Can violence ever be justified in resisting oppression? The show turned pulp material into genuine occasions for thinking about nihilism, friendship, and punishment.
005 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosop: The Lord of the Rings is Tolkien's monumental 1950s fantasy epic of hobbits, wizards, and a quest to destroy a ring of absolute power, beloved worldwide and famously filmed by Peter Jackson. Its central device is a philosophical thought experiment: Plato's Ring of Gyges, which grants impunity. Would anyone remain just? From Gollum to Galadriel to Frodo at the Crack of Doom, Tolkien dramatizes how unlimited power corrupts. The essays also mine Middle-earth for answers on happiness, friendship, fetishism, and joy amid sorrow.
006 - Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking: Baseball, America's old pastoral ballgame of bats, bases, and endless statistics, has generated more argument than any other sport, which makes it fertile philosophical ground. What does it mean to sacrifice with a bunt? Is rooting for the perpetually losing Cubs a form of religious faith? Do the rules themselves contain contradictions? The essays here weigh cheating and sportsmanship through Kant and Aristotle, umpire discretion through Austin and Dworkin, and even what the ballpark's 'home' says about belonging.
007 - The Sopranos and Philosophy - I Ki: The Sopranos (1999-2007) is the celebrated HBO drama about Tony Soprano, a New Jersey mob boss who begins seeing a therapist while running a criminal family alongside his real one. It invites philosophy because it is an existential drama disguised as a gangster story: why does a man with everything feel like a loser? Can Tony's code of honor survive his own appetites? Is he a Machiavellian prince, a Nietzschean nihilist sunk in resentment, or just an 'ethical manager' of a murderous business?
008 - Woody Allen and Philosophy - You M: Woody Allen is the American filmmaker and comedian whose anxious, joke-laden films of the 1970s through 1990s, from Annie Hall to Crimes and Misdemeanors, made neurosis and moral panic entertaining. His characters are philosophy generators: If nothing in the universe is permanent, can life have meaning? Is integrity more than consistency? Can Judah murder and get away with it in a world without God? The essays take his comedies seriously as arguments about despair, faith, hedonism, and how to appreciate art.
009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If A: Harry Potter is J.K. Rowling's seven-novel fantasy series (1997-2007) about a boy wizard at Hogwarts school, the best-selling book series in history. Rowling, like Tolkien and Lewis, poses real philosophical problems for young readers: What is a soul, and can Voldemort's Horcruxes really split one? Does prophecy, such as the one marking Harry as the Chosen One, leave any room for free choice? Is love the most powerful magic? The essays test the wizarding world against ancient and modern theories of mind, identity, and destiny.
010 - Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosoph: The Passion of the Christ (2004) is Mel Gibson's brutally graphic film of Jesus's final twelve hours, one of the highest-grossing religious films ever made and an instant lightning rod for controversy. Because its subject is God incarnate suffering, its questions cut deeper than most movie philosophy: Why did Christ have to die so violently, and what does atonement mean? Is the film anti-Semitic? Can Judas be blamed for a betrayal God foreknew? Is the gore a route to the sublime or a distortion of the whole person?
012 - Star Wars and Philosophy - More Po: Star Wars is George Lucas's epoch-making space-fantasy saga (from 1977) of the Skywalker family, the evil Empire, and the mystical Force, one of the most beloved film series ever made. Its black-and-white conflict hides surprisingly rich questions: Are Anakin and Luke really free if a prophecy foretold their fates? Is Yoda a Stoic sage, and the Jedi path a kind of Zen? Is Lando's betrayal of Han a defensible utilitarian choice? The essays trace virtue, evil, and destiny through a galaxy far, far away.
